name: Digi-Key

claims.claim_text: Catalog distribution functions as a gate on component selection: a part that cannot be bought in small quantities from a major catalog distributor will not be designed in, because prototype builds cannot be supplied. A semiconductor startup that launches without distributor listings therefore forecloses its own design-ins regardless of the merits of the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: If it can't get the prototype, no one's putting it in their final design
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: BASIC, Chip companies & Robots - Pernicious Projects, Puppies in Peril

claims.claim_text: Getting listed by a catalog distributor is a negotiated relationship rather than a form submission, taking a courtship of several months and requiring the supplier to satisfy the distributor that it will be a viable line. The distributor buys reel quantities up front because its model depends on shipping from its own stock anywhere in the world within about forty-eight hours, which is defeated if it has to call the manufacturer for each order.
claims.quote_verbatim: That was a several-month courtship that went on between us and them to make that happen
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: Distributor parametric search is the ordinary first step in part selection for a design engineer, resolving the search about ninety-five percent of the time before the manufacturers' own sites are consulted.
claims.quote_verbatim: 95% of the time, bang, I'm going to find a suitable part on DigiKey, parametric search every time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: The limit of distributor parametric search is that its filters cover catalogue attributes rather than application requirements, so a search for an unusual specification such as a charger for a very low capacity cell, outside the several-hundred-milliamp to several-amp band where most parts are made, has to be conducted on manufacturers' own sites instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: DigiKey and Mouser won't have that search capability
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Autorouter, Datasheets & Obscure Chips - Cloddish Collegiate Conversations

claims.claim_text: The scale of the device space defeats catalogue filtering on its own: one survey of analog-to-digital converters counted 2,412 devices from 24 manufacturers, roughly a hundred parts per manufacturer, which is why the distributor's filters cannot substitute for manufacturer selection guides.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's 2,412 ADC devices on the market from 24 different manufacturers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chairs, Sparks and Devices - Optional Olent Obreption

claims.claim_text: Parametric searches on both distributor and manufacturer sites silently omit parts that would have qualified, so a search result should be treated as a sample rather than as an exhaustive list, and an experienced colleague naming a part they have already used remains the faster route.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can easily miss parts doing the parametric searches
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Faced with thousands of qualifying results, the common resolution is to sort by price and take the cheapest, a shortcut that reliably selects a poor part. Two heuristics reduce the field more usefully: pin count implies feature set, since a three-pin regulator physically cannot have a shutdown input, and sorting or filtering by manufacturer uses brand as a proxy for trust.
claims.quote_verbatim: you drill down in the parametric search and you go, right, that one's in salt by price
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Radiation Chips & Old Package Types - Technocratic Toilet Troubleshooting

claims.claim_text: A designer without corporate part-approval constraints can invert the selection process and design only around parts currently in distributor stock, which removes obsolescence risk from the design and lets components and bare boards be ordered at the same moment. The same inversion at the level of cost, sorting a low-cost catalogue by price to find a one-cent regulator and a three-cent microcontroller, generates the product concept from the achievable bill-of-materials cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can design around the parts you can actually get
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Harrison - X-ray Examining Xenogogue

claims.claim_text: Processor selection for a cost-sensitive product can be made directly from the distributor listing by taking the cheapest part meeting the requirement, with the caveat that which device holds that position changes over time.
claims.quote_verbatim: I went to DigiKey and I had a look which one is the cheapest one
claims.speaker: Robert Feranec

claims.claim_text: Catalog distributor prices carry a premium that pays for holding stock and breaking bulk, so a part listed at ten dollars may be three or four dollars bought in volume direct. The premium collapses at reel quantities: a reel of five thousand parts costs about the same from a catalog distributor as from the manufacturer, and the gap only reopens at volumes on the order of a million.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of that money is going straight to Digikey for holding that part for you
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The recommended costing method for a new product prices the bill of materials at catalog distributor rates and assumes local assembly, then applies the conventional three to four times margin multiplier. Any saving obtained later by moving manufacture offshore is upside rather than a requirement, whereas a plan that assumes lowest-cost offshore manufacture from the outset leaves no options if that route becomes unavailable.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you base it on local assembly costs, which you can get and DigiKey pricing, you're fairly safe
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: A standard-cost convention makes bill-of-materials estimates comparable: the thousand-piece distributor price is recorded as a field on each part in the design tool and used as the budgetary figure handed to a client, on the explicit understanding that it is not what will be paid and that shipping and other loadings sit on top.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm basically putting a field in KiCad saying standard cost. And then I just go and grab the 1K price

claims.claim_text: A bill of materials kept in a spreadsheet is obsolete the moment it is finished and cannot express the things that actually govern purchasing: multiple currencies across a multinational supply chain, minimum order quantities, order multiples, parts shared between several projects that should be bought together, and approved substitutes. A database-backed tool defers the choice between substitutes to the moment of ordering, so the decision is made against what the market actually has that day.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have your bomb in a spreadsheet, basically stop doing it

claims.claim_text: The purchasing workflow that follows from that model is a cart of several bills of materials multiplied by their build quantities, collapsed into a combined purchase list that still holds unresolved meta-parts; the offers available at that moment are then selected from, manually or by rules such as preferring one distributor and falling through to others on unavailability, and only then does the list become an order for specific part numbers.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would like to buy everything from DigiKey. And then if they don't have it available, I would like to go to Mazer

claims.claim_text: Single-piece price curves are steeper for FPGAs than for other devices, with single-unit prices around a hundred and fifty dollars, because holding cost is high and single-quantity demand is low. Some manufacturers additionally restrict volume distribution to one authorised distributor for export-compliance reasons, so the catalog listing exists for prototypes while production goes elsewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: single piece price is like $150 for a chip
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Distribution is a thin-margin, high-churn business rather than a high-margin one: an annual report showing a billion dollars of revenue against about fifty million of profit puts net margin around five percent, and the model depends on volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: Our revenues are a billion dollars
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Layout, CAD & Raspberry Pi - Kedogenous Kinetic Knowledge

claims.claim_text: Per-line handling charges dominate small builds in a way that unit prices conceal: a reeling charge of about seven dollars per part is unremarkable once, but a design with fifty unique parts adds several hundred dollars, and international shipping on a handful of modules can double their effective unit cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: seven bucks per reel doesn't sound that bad in single quantities, but if you have 50 uniques
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Expedited shipping is cheap measured against the cost of not having parts, and the rate a distributor passes on is below what an individual can negotiate because of their courier volume: overnight delivery at around thirty dollars, against roughly a hundred for first-thing-in-the-morning service.
claims.quote_verbatim: DigiKey overnight is like 30 bucks UPS or FedEx
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Buying through authorised distribution is the practical defence against counterfeit and re-marked components, since grey-market supply carries a substantial chance of receiving a package correctly marked on the outside with a different die inside, which for an analog part means the wrong function entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's the advantage of buying from, you know, Mauser, DigiKey and Farnells and, you know, authorized distributors
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The risk from an unverified source scales with how hard the part is to validate on receipt: an LED is tested by turning it on, whereas a microcontroller cannot be qualified by inspection, so the same supply route is acceptable for one and not the other.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it's an LED, your test is, does it turn on?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Authorised supply does not eliminate part-identity errors. A batch ordered as 0.1 percent tolerance resistors arrived as one percent parts under the correct part number, reached assembled boards and shipped before the discrepancy was found during testing of the following batch, with the fault traced towards the component manufacturer rather than the distributor.
claims.quote_verbatim: the resistor isn't 0.1%. It's a couple of percent
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The Chinese catalog distributor that Western engineers encounter occupies the same tier of trust as the established catalog distributors for sourcing purposes, because it is an official supplier for the brands it lists and does not substitute; the difference is the brand mix, which includes Asian manufacturers unfamiliar elsewhere. Marketplace platforms carry no such guarantee.
claims.quote_verbatim: they are an official supplier for those brands, just like Mouser and DigiKey are
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Marketplace listings, in which third-party sellers offer stock inside a distributor's catalogue, undercut the guarantee that brings engineers to that distributor in the first place. A search returning a seller's own warehouse rather than distributor-held stock is not what the buyer went there for, and distinguishing the two in the interface becomes a requirement rather than a preference.
claims.quote_verbatim: the reason I go to DigiKey is because I want DigiKey stock
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Publicly visible distributor stock levels function as market intelligence: a stock figure that never moves is evidence that a product sold nothing, and scraping catalogue stock across vendors produces a picture of which manufacturers actually have supply.
claims.quote_verbatim: the stock on DigiKey is always the same. It never went down
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: During a shortage, aggregate catalogue stock figures are misleading, because sorting a manufacturer's parts by stock level surfaces exactly the lines that are well supplied rather than the ones that are short. A shortage has to be diagnosed part by part.
claims.quote_verbatim: I sorted by stock level and I'm going, well, there's 57,000, there's 40,000, there's 30,000
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Parts shown as on order are not reserved: another buyer can take the whole incoming quantity before it lands, so a promised arrival date carries no entitlement and committing cash early to hold a position is a cash-flow problem rather than a guarantee. Stock that appears can also be gone within minutes of being noticed.
claims.quote_verbatim: If someone swoops in and buys all those parts underneath me, like I'm screwed
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Distributors forward obsolescence notices to customers who have bought the affected part, but the more reliable practice is to re-quote the whole bill of materials every few months, since the quoting process itself surfaces parts that have become unbuyable.
claims.quote_verbatim: run your bomb every couple months make sure they can actually buy the parts
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Catalog distributor stock is not a production supply. A few thousand parts looks abundant to a designer but is consumed immediately once multiplied by parts per board and boards per run, and past a modest volume threshold the only route is buying reels directly from the manufacturer. Quantities on the order of a million cannot be bought through distribution at all, with the partial exception of the cheapest passives.
claims.quote_verbatim: DigiKey is actually not enough volume. So you start buying reels from the manufacturer
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: An assembly run cannot begin until every line on the bill of materials is in hand, so a single backordered passive stops the entire job regardless of the value of the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: if digi-key is backordered on a resistor, it's like, well, that's right. Wait until that resistor gets here
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Lead time on a needed part is often identical at the distributor and at the manufacturer, and no volume commitment buys priority; the answer given to a customer asking to be moved up the queue is to plan further ahead next time.
claims.quote_verbatim: is there any volume that I can give you that will bump me up the priority list
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The floor on semiconductor lead time is structural rather than commercial: roughly thirty days of wafer processing, then shipment to another country for packaging, then further test, then distribution, which makes six weeks an optimistic minimum even before material for the wafer starts is considered. A demand surge propagates through that chain the way a traffic jam clears, in stop-start waves rather than smoothly.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was like a 30 day start to finish, you know, wafer in, wafer out
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Semiconductors developed to one large customer's requirement were historically released into general distribution afterwards, so the repair trade could buy them. Increasingly they are not, leaving no legitimate supply at all; the resulting practice of buying new assemblies purely to remove one chip and discard the rest is the cost of that closure.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're actually at the point of buying charging cases
claims.speaker: Louis Rossmann
claims.episode_title: Right To Repair with Louis Rossmann

claims.claim_text: The distribution tiers perform different functions. Catalog distributors hold large physical inventories and sell in small quantities; the large authorised distributors increasingly hold little or no stock and operate principally as financing intermediaries between manufacturer and customer, which is a real service but not a stocking one.
claims.quote_verbatim: primarily act as banks, but then you go to like, uh, you know, like a digi key
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: Late-evening order cut-offs with next-morning delivery change how prototyping is scheduled, since a part discovered missing at seven on a Friday evening can be on the bench the following morning. The assumption fails completely outside the served region: shipping to South America took a week at best, three dollars of cable attracted two hundred and fifty dollars of freight plus customs duty, and the working response is to plan ahead rather than to order reactively.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fastest I can get something to Chile, um, is a week
claims.speaker: Greg Gage
claims.episode_title: An interview with Greg and Tim of Backyard Brains - Boethetic Bug Brainwaves

claims.claim_text: International shipping charges from large distributors are high because their fulfilment is built entirely around couriers, with no path for ordinary postal dispatch; smaller vendors shipping the same item by post charge a fraction of the amount but take far longer.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can't afford to have somebody go down to the post office, stand in line
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer - Comical Keyzer Comes a-Callin'

claims.claim_text: Orders shipped from the United States require an end-use declaration covering military, government surveillance and nuclear or chemical weapons applications, and a declaration of personal use can still trigger a follow-up request for details of the project, even for an order of passive components.
claims.quote_verbatim: we need more details on your project. What exactly are these parts going to be used in?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The same export-control regime that produces those declarations restricts specific technologies to specific destinations, and some components cannot be bought at all without signing an export control agreement, which can defeat a purchase entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to sign an export control agreement
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Noah Feehan - Biloquistic Blinking Blush

claims.claim_text: Tariffs are itemised on distributor invoices and applied to imported components. Where duty falls on raw components but not on finished goods, the structure penalises domestic assembly directly, since importing parts to build locally attracts the charge while importing the completed product does not.
claims.quote_verbatim: there were tariffs on like raw components, but not on finished goods

claims.claim_text: Design tools embed distributor catalogues so that a part can be pulled into a schematic by parametric search or by part number, complete with symbol and footprint. Coverage is the limiting factor: early implementations were missing footprints for less common parts such as connectors, and a distributor-published open-source library covered on the order of a thousand parts because it was produced by hand.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got the DigiKey parametric search built right in there
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: PCB Mills, SDR and Oscilloscopes - Flaunting Furbelow Fanciness

claims.claim_text: Distributor-derived libraries are necessarily atomic, binding one footprint, one symbol and one 3D model to a single orderable part number, because two orderable variants of the same device can carry entirely different packages and must therefore be separate entries in both schematic and layout.
claims.quote_verbatim: atomic being like a one footprint, one symbol, one 3D model
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Cross-distributor aggregators exist to search stock and pricing across vendors at once, and design tools consume a mixture of aggregator APIs, direct feeds from several distributors, and data taken directly from semiconductor manufacturers, because no single source is complete or reliable enough on its own.
claims.quote_verbatim: we also work with DigiKey and Arrow and Newark and Mouser, um, to get data more directly
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Distributor APIs give reliable access to catalogue data but uneven access to ordering, with the level of integration depending on the account, so a workable compromise is generating a purchase order locally and uploading it. Anti-scraping countermeasures intended to distinguish humans from bulk scrapers also block legitimate automated tooling, since the two are hard to tell apart.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's varying levels of integration with the APIs
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: AI Tooling with Matt Liberty and Luke Beno

claims.claim_text: Component inventory management keys on distributor barcodes: scanning a bag recovers the manufacturer part number and, from modern two-dimensional codes, the quantity, but never the storage location, so a location scheme remains the operator's responsibility. Embedding order-specific identifiers in the purchase order closes the loop, because the labels printed on despatch then identify the line item and quantity on receipt.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can connect a USB barcode scanner to parts box

claims.claim_text: The discipline that makes an inventory system work is that unrecorded parts are treated as lost, since they will not be found and will be bought again; after an initial indexing effort, maintaining it costs a few minutes per order.
claims.quote_verbatim: the parts that I haven't entered into parts box, they're considered lost

claims.claim_text: Printing the part number and values onto the back of cut tape replaces the practice of hand-marking each strip with a permanent marker, which is the step that made small-quantity tape orders identifiable on the bench.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're now printing the DigiKey part number and the values and stuff, the details on the back of the cut tape
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Thermally printed component bag labels faded to blank over time, which destroys the identification of anything stored in its original packaging; the defect was acknowledged and corrected in later labels.
claims.quote_verbatim: all the digi key labels are freaking worn off
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Multicopter, DIY drones & Tektronix - Zappy Zendik Zoilism

claims.claim_text: Loading a complete bill of materials into the distributor's own system turns reordering into a single operation that computes the correct quantities and reports stock availability against every line before the order is placed, which is the practical argument for concentrating a build's purchasing with one supplier even at a higher unit price.
claims.quote_verbatim: it tells you live in the bomb whether or not I have stock
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: Published price breaks stop well below production quantities, so a buyer needing one thousand to a hundred thousand pieces must request a quote by email and wait days, when the pricing follows a formula the distributor could apply instantly against a logged-in account with its discounts already known.
claims.quote_verbatim: I want to be able to say, I need a thousand of this part. And I don't want to have to send an email
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Two bills of materials are maintained for the same design because the part numbers differ by packaging: a production version specifying reels and a separate short-run version specifying cut tape for hand assembly.
claims.quote_verbatim: One will be a production BOM spreadsheet and another one will be
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Motors And Upgrading Sinclairs - Adapting Apraxiated Automobiles

claims.claim_text: Some oscillator parts are programmed to order by the distributor rather than stocked at every frequency, which resolves an inventory-breadth problem that would otherwise require carrying every value in the range along with its packaging variants.
claims.quote_verbatim: DigiKey or some distributors actually program them to order some of these MEMS
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Repackaging components from bulk into forms suited to short runs is a recognised gap in the supply chain. Cut-tape services address part of it, and automated de-reeling into trays would address more, but the process carries real cost with no guaranteed demand.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're going to basically automate this system where we're derailing resistors
claims.speaker: Jonathan Hirschman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: Part availability propagates into physical assembly problems that are invisible at selection time: constrained to whichever LED the distributor had in quantity, a build found the carrier tape so thin that parts were ejected as the feeder advanced.
claims.quote_verbatim: we could only use the stuff that DigiKey had enough stock of
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Wholly off-the-shelf sourcing is itself a competitive exposure: a product built entirely from parts anyone can order carries no supply-chain position and nothing that cannot be reproduced by a competitor who takes it apart, so differentiation has to come from somewhere other than the parts list.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you can buy it, it's not specialized
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The existence of hundreds of thousands of fully characterised, tested and qualified parts in multiple packages at prices of cents each is the benchmark any on-demand chip fabrication method has to clear, and it is the packaging, test and qualification rather than the patterning that constitutes the difficulty.
claims.quote_verbatim: you haven't packaged it you haven't tested it you haven't qualified it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: We'll Believe It When We See It - Hiring Hypercatalectic Helpelp

claims.claim_text: The same availability threshold is applied as a test of whether a technology is real: an announced device is treated as not existing until it can be ordered from a catalog distributor, which is also the point at which a novel processor architecture becomes usable in a product.
claims.quote_verbatim: until you can buy it in DigiKey, it doesn't exist
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Catalogue searches also settle questions about package obsolescence empirically: filtering the distributor's chip listings by through-hole packages returns tens of thousands of parts, a figure that has declined only slightly over a decade, which is evidence against the recurring prediction that such packages are about to disappear.
claims.quote_verbatim: search how many are available in a dip package
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor manufacturers keep decades-old parts in production because a design that specified one twenty or thirty years ago still needs supply, and the continued catalogue listing of long-obsolete devices is the visible result of that lifecycle obligation.
claims.quote_verbatim: they still make the same micro. Because somebody designed it into a product 20 or even 30 years ago
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Local component markets carry information that catalogues do not: a catalogue lists every part but does not distinguish which parts are commonly used and available at manufacturing scale in a given region. A part list drawn purely from Western catalogue numbers came back from a Chinese assembler as unbuildable in the normal way, with cheaper and more available local equivalents substituted. The information can be approximated remotely by translating the part category and searching a Chinese marketplace sorted by popularity.
claims.quote_verbatim: what it doesn't tell you is like, which of these parts is common
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: A Chinese catalog distributor tied to a board fabricator exposes parts that are only available in that market, which is where an equivalent part number for an unfamiliar Asian-marked component can be found.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can actually find that equivalent part number if you search LCSC
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Search result ordering at a distributor is a question worth knowing the answer to, because a paid ranking would silently bias part discovery. The distributors differ: some do sell placement, and the largest catalog distributor was confirmed not to.
claims.quote_verbatim: There are some sites that do it, but, uh, DigiKey is not one of them
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Stock listings that prove wrong on ordering are the failure that damages a distributor's usefulness most directly, because the whole reason for using one is the assurance that a part shown as in stock will actually arrive.
claims.quote_verbatim: they promote that they have parts and then they do not
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Large customers hold blanket purchase orders with catalog distributors, so buying a piece of equipment through that distributor bypasses the approved-vendor process entirely. For a small supplier, being listed removes a procurement barrier that has nothing to do with the merits of the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: they just have like a blanket PO with DigiKey

claims.claim_text: Catalog distributors fund technical education directly, commissioning and hosting full course series on their own channels and publishing an industry magazine written by outside contributors, which is a marketing channel operating as a component of the design ecosystem rather than as advertising.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm contracted with DigiKey to produce
claims.speaker: Shawn Hymel

claims.claim_text: Component warehousing is physically unglamorous and largely manual: rows of steel shelving holding cardboard trays with barcodes on the front, walked by pickers who pull the tray, take the parts and replace it, with temporary as well as permanent labour on the line.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's got like these steel shelves with these little cardboard trays with a barcode on the front
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Best way to find a leak

claims.claim_text: The dominant catalog distributor's location was chosen by accident of origin rather than logistics, being far from a major airport or transport infrastructure, which forces it to operate its own inbound courier arrangements and to bus in several thousand employees from surrounding towns.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is the worst possible place to put it because there's no major airport
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chris Becomes Self Employed - Quixotic Quitting Quaere

attribution_notes: ep 38, 163, 204, 458, 527, 542, 645 and 699 sit on the unreliable-attribution list or carry fused turns; those claims are attributed by content with no speaker name.
Reception and sentiment material about the distributor, of which the bundle contains a great deal, was excluded under the knowledge-only rule.
